rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its strongest line, "How big does a purchase have to be before Pay by Bank beats a card?", turns Plaid's own 70% claim into a reporter-shaped analysis piece without pretending the missing fee schedule exists. B is sharper in places, especially "Plaid needs 12,000 banks to help route payments past the fees banks collect," but that angle leans on inferred bank economics and supplied-no-one facts dressed as a story premise.
gaps_in_A: "Plaid turns 12,000 bank connections into a payments network" is refused as a duplicate too quickly; the bank/institution-side tension may be a separate trade angle if proven.

"Next step: journalist-fit-check for the counterposition angle, which is the only one that can run on the launch facts alone" undersells the FedNow infrastructure angle, which can run if Plaid can answer reach and rail questions.
The set never fully develops the bank-side protagonist; it asks "Has any bank partner said anything on record" but parks a potentially useful angle instead of framing it conditionally.
gaps_in_B: "FedNow adoption stories have mostly been about disbursements and B2B" is outside the supplied update. It may be true, but in this exercise it is an invented peg unless sourced.
"The prevailing belief in the category is that pay-by-bank is a general-purpose card replacement" is another unsupported market claim. The 70% math angle does not need that decoration.

"Plaid needs 12,000 banks to help route payments past the fees banks collect" is useful but rests on inferred issuing-bank revenue impact; B admits this later, which means the headline is ahead of the proof.
"four viable shapes exist" is too generous. The bank-side angle is a conditional lead, not viable until Plaid can confirm opt-in, economics, and a bank source.
